question:
Select the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
I will never overlook this creativity.
option_1: This creativity will never be overlooked by me.
option_2: This creativity will be overlooked by me.
option_3: This creativity will being overlooked by me.
option_4: This creativity will not never be overlooked by me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. This creativity will never be overlooked by me.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "I will never overlook this creativity" is in the Simple Future Tense with the negative adverb "never".

• Rule — Passive Voice of Simple Future Tense (with an adverb like "never"):
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + (adverb) + V1 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + (adverb) + be + V3 + by + Subject
◦ The adverb "never" keeps its position, coming after the modal "will" and before "be".

• Applying the rule: the object "this creativity" becomes the subject; "overlook" becomes the past participle "overlooked"; "I" becomes the agent "me" with "by"; and "never" stays right after "will".
◦ Passive: This creativity will never be overlooked by me.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it drops the negative adverb "never", which completely reverses the meaning of the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "will being overlooked" is grammatically wrong; the passive requires the base form "be" after the modal "will", not "being".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will not never" is a double negative and is grammatically unacceptable in Standard English.

NOTE

• In passive constructions with modals (will/can/must/may), the structure is always modal + be + V3; never use "being" or "been" here.

• Adverbs of frequency/negation such as never, always, often are placed immediately after the first auxiliary/modal verb in both active and passive sentences.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A place where birds are kept
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Aviary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Aviary" means a large enclosure or cage in which birds are kept. (पक्षीशाला/पक्षियों को रखने का बाड़ा)
◦ Example: The zoo's aviary houses over fifty species of exotic birds.

• The word comes from the Latin "avis", meaning bird, the same root found in words like aviation and aviator.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Zoo (चिड़ियाघर): A place where a wide variety of wild animals (not just birds) are kept for public viewing.

• Option 3: Sanctuary (अभयारण्य): A large, often natural, protected area where wildlife in general is protected from hunting or danger.

• Option 4: Hive (छत्ता): A structure, natural or man-made, in which bees live and store honey.

NOTE

• Other related one-word substitutions frequently asked in SSC exams: Aquarium (a place where fish are kept), Apiary (a place where bees are kept), Kennel (a place where dogs are kept), Stable (a place where horses are kept).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Catastrophe
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Success.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Catastrophe" means a sudden event that causes great damage or suffering; a disaster. (विपत्ति/तबाही)
◦ Example: The flood was a catastrophe for the entire village.

• Its antonym is "Success", meaning the accomplishment of an aim or a favourable outcome. (सफलता)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Nurture (पालन-पोषण करना): To care for and encourage the growth or development of someone or something; unrelated in meaning to catastrophe.

• Option 3: Immaculate (निष्कलंक/स्वच्छ): Perfectly clean, neat, or without any flaws; not connected to the idea of disaster.

• Option 4: Disaster (आपदा): This is a synonym, not an antonym, of catastrophe — both mean a calamity.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of catastrophe: calamity, tragedy, cataclysm, misfortune.

• Other antonyms of catastrophe: triumph, blessing, boon, fortune.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Beyond skills, experience, and training, companies search for applicants who display excitement — those they believe shall carry out allocated responsibilities cheerfully and cooperatively.
option_1: shall take up any designated obligations
option_4: should pick up all skills and works
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. will execute assigned duties.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "shall carry out allocated responsibilities" must be replaced by an option that keeps the same meaning, tense, and modal sense as the original sentence.

• "Will execute assigned duties" correctly conveys the same idea — an applicant who will perform (execute) the duties (responsibilities) given (assigned/allocated) to them — in natural, grammatically correct English.

• Rule — Sentence Substitution: the replacement must not add, drop, or distort any part of the original meaning, and must remain grammatically parallel to the rest of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "any designated obligations" changes the meaning — the original specifies allocated (assigned) responsibilities, not "any" obligation in general.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "will demonstrate non-biased work" introduces a completely new idea (impartiality) that is not present in the original sentence at all.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "should pick up all skills and works" distorts the meaning — the original is about carrying out allocated responsibilities, not acquiring "all skills and works".

NOTE

• In sentence-substitution questions, always check three things: (1) meaning is preserved, (2) tense/modal is preserved, and (3) the resulting sentence is grammatically correct and natural.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
After years of fights with his neighbour Ram, Shekhar decided to hold out the _______ and invited Ram for tea.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. olive branch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to hold out/extend the olive branch" means to offer peace or reconciliation to someone after a conflict. (शांति और सुलह का प्रस्ताव देना)
◦ Example: After the argument, she held out an olive branch by inviting her friend for coffee.

• The idiom fits the context perfectly — after years of fighting, Shekhar invited Ram for tea, a clear act of reconciliation.

• The expression originates from ancient tradition, where an olive branch was a symbol of peace.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Poker face (निर्भाव मुख): An expression that reveals no emotion or true feeling; unrelated to reconciliation.

• Option 2: Comparing apples to oranges (असंगत तुलना करना): Refers to comparing two things that are fundamentally different and not comparable; does not fit the context.

• Option 3: Chip on shoulder (मन में द्वेष रखना): Means to hold a grudge or resentment — the opposite of what Shekhar is shown doing.

NOTE

• Other idioms of peace/reconciliation often asked in SSC: "bury the hatchet", "make peace with", and "let bygones be bygones".

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Countemptible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Contemptible" — deserving of contempt or scorn; despicable.
◦ Example: His contemptible behaviour towards the staff shocked everyone.

• Spelling key: CON + TEMPT + IBLE (from the word "contempt"). The given word wrongly inserts an extra "u" ("Coun-" instead of "Con-").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Centenary" is correctly spelt — it means a hundredth anniversary.

• Option 2: "Consumerist" is correctly spelt — relating to consumerism.

• Option 3: "Capitalist" is correctly spelt — a supporter of or believer in capitalism.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "contemptible" (deserving contempt) with "contemptuous" (showing contempt).

• Other tricky spellings with silent/extra letters commonly tested: embarrass, questionnaire, occurrence, harass.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
One must be very strong to lift this box of glass jars.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Weak.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Strong" means having great physical power or force. (शक्तिशाली/मज़बूत)

• Its antonym is "Weak", meaning lacking physical strength or power. (कमज़ोर)
◦ Example: He felt too weak to carry the heavy box after the illness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Mighty (शक्तिशाली): This is a synonym of "strong", not its antonym.

• Option 3: Complicated (जटिल): Means difficult or intricate; it is unrelated to physical strength.

• Option 4: Rugged (मज़बूत/ऊबड़-खाबड़): Means tough, sturdy, or having a rough terrain; it is close to a synonym of strong, not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of strong: robust, sturdy, powerful, forceful.

• Other antonyms of strong: feeble, frail, fragile, delicate.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.

Anand personally believes in the motto, "When life gives you lemons, make lemonade."
option_1: Earn the maximum out of business
option_3: Enjoy the most when the season is favourable
option_4: Make the best out of difficult situations
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Make the best out of difficult situations.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "When life gives you lemons, make lemonade" means to make the best of a difficult or unfavourable situation, turning a setback into something positive. (विपरीत परिस्थितियों में भी सर्वोत्तम करना)
◦ Example: She lost her job, but she used the free time to start her own business — truly making lemonade out of lemons.

• Sour, bitter lemons (a hardship) are transformed into sweet, refreshing lemonade (a positive outcome) — this is the core image behind the idiom.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Earn the maximum out of business — this is unrelated; the idiom is not specifically about business profit.

• Option 2: Nourish health — this is unrelated; the idiom has nothing to do with health or nourishment.

• Option 3: Enjoy the most when the season is favourable — this is actually the opposite sense; the idiom is specifically about coping well when circumstances are unfavourable, not favourable.

NOTE

• Other idioms with a similar meaning of resilience/optimism: "every cloud has a silver lining", "turn a negative into a positive", and "make a virtue of necessity".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Monotonous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Engrossing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Monotonous" means dull, repetitive, and lacking in variety or interest. (नीरस/उबाऊ)

• Its antonym is "Engrossing", meaning absorbing all one's attention and interest; captivating. (दिलचस्प/तल्लीन कर देने वाला)
◦ Example: The novel was so engrossing that she finished it in one sitting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Tiresome (उबाऊ): This is a synonym of monotonous, meaning boring or wearisome, not its antonym.

• Option 2: Tedious (थकाऊ): This is also a synonym of monotonous, meaning long and dull, not its antonym.

• Option 4: Rational (तर्कसंगत): Means logical or based on reason; it is unrelated in meaning to monotonous.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of monotonous: dull, humdrum, repetitive, drab.

• Other antonyms of monotonous: exciting, varied, interesting, stimulating.

question:
Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
You need to be concious enough to listen to the question.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. concious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Conscious" — aware of and responding to one's surroundings; awake and alert.
◦ Example: He remained conscious throughout the surgery.

• Spelling key: CON + SCI + OUS — note the letters "s" and "c" together ("sci"), which are commonly swapped or dropped by mistake, as in the incorrect "concious".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "enough" is correctly spelt.

• Option 3: "question" is correctly spelt.

• Option 4: "listen" is correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "conscious" (aware) with "conscience" (a person's moral sense of right and wrong).

• Other commonly misspelled words: unconscious, subconscious, conscientious.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym to replace the underlined word in the given sentence.
How did we end up in this rapturous situation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. ecstatic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Rapturous" means feeling or expressing great pleasure, joy, or enthusiasm. (अत्यंत हर्षित/आनंदमग्न)
◦ Example: The crowd gave the singer a rapturous welcome.

• Its synonym is "Ecstatic", meaning feeling or expressing overwhelming happiness or joyful excitement. (अत्यानंदित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: terrifying (भयानक): Means causing great fear; this is nearly opposite in meaning to "rapturous".

• Option 3: misleading (भ्रामक): Means giving a false or wrong impression; unrelated to the joyful sense of "rapturous".

• Option 4: disastrous (विनाशकारी): Means causing great damage; again, nearly opposite in meaning to "rapturous".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of rapturous: elated, euphoric, overjoyed, thrilled, blissful.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The mother asked the child, "Will you tell me who did accompany you to the airport?"
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. who accompanied you.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "who did accompany you" occurs inside an embedded/indirect question ("Will you tell me...").

• Rule — Embedded Questions with a Wh-word as Subject: when the wh-word (who/what/which) itself is the subject of the clause, the auxiliary do/does/did is NOT used; the main verb simply takes the required tense directly.
◦ Correct: who accompanied you (Simple Past, no "did")
◦ Incorrect: who did accompany you

• Since the context refers to a completed past action (accompanying the child to the airport), the simple past form "accompanied" is required.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "who accompanies you" is incorrect because it is in the Simple Present Tense, but the context clearly refers to a past event.

• Option 2: "who does accompany you" is incorrect for two reasons — it wrongly uses do-support with a subject wh-word, and it is in the wrong (present) tense.

• Option 4: "who must be accompanied you" is incorrect because it is an ungrammatical, garbled construction that mixes passive and active forms.

NOTE

• Compare: "Who did you meet?" (correct — "who" is the object, so do-support IS needed) vs. "Who met you?" (correct — "who" is the subject, so do-support is NOT needed). The same rule applies inside embedded/indirect questions.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the sentences in the correct sequence to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A)This past summer, my dream finally came true.
B)Strange lands, exciting places, and new cultures have always fascinated me.
C)Ever since I was a little girl, I dreamed about travelling overseas.
D)I got to travel to England, France, Switzerland, and Germany.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. CBAD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C is the ideal opener — it introduces the writer as a little girl who dreamed of travelling overseas, setting up the background of the paragraph.

• Sentence B logically follows C, elaborating on why she had that childhood dream — she was always fascinated by strange lands, exciting places, and new cultures.

• Sentence A follows next, showing the turning point — "This past summer, my dream finally came true" — moving the paragraph from childhood dream to present-day fulfilment.

• Sentence D logically concludes the paragraph, giving the specific details of the trip (England, France, Switzerland, and Germany) that resulted from the dream coming true.

• Rule — Paragraph Coherence: the correct order must move logically from background/context to elaboration to the main event to specific supporting detail, with pronouns and time references ("my dream", "this past summer") linking correctly to what precedes them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (CBAD).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DCBA) is incorrect because it starts with the specific travel details (D) before establishing any context for why the writer travelled at all.

• Option 3 (ABCD) is incorrect because it starts with "This past summer, my dream finally came true" (A) before the reader even knows what the dream was, making it confusing.

• Option 4 (BADC) is incorrect because it places B before the origin of the fascination (C) is established, breaking the logical cause-effect flow.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look for the sentence that best introduces the topic (usually contains no pronoun referring backward) as the starting sentence, and trace pronouns/connectors (this, it, my dream) to link the rest.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Rectify
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. amend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Rectify" means to put right or correct something that is wrong. (सुधारना/ठीक करना)
◦ Example: The company promised to rectify the billing error immediately.

• Its synonym is "Amend", meaning to make minor changes to something in order to correct or improve it. (संशोधित करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: mar (बिगाड़ना): Means to spoil or damage the appearance/quality of something — this is nearly opposite to rectify.

• Option 3: corrupt (भ्रष्ट करना): Means to cause to become dishonest or to spoil the purity of something — this is not the meaning of rectify.

• Option 4: upset (परेशान करना): Means to disturb or make someone unhappy — unrelated to the sense of correcting an error.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of rectify: correct, remedy, fix, redress, set right.

• Word family: rectification (noun), rectifiable (adjective).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
To __________ the ticket, Amith had to visit the travel agency many times.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. confirm.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Confirm" means to make certain or establish the validity of something, such as a booking or reservation. (पुष्टि करना)
◦ Example: Please confirm your ticket at least 24 hours before departure.

• "Confirm the ticket" is a natural, commonly used collocation in the context of travel bookings, which fits the sentence perfectly — Amith visited the agency repeatedly to get his ticket confirmed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: contract (अनुबंध करना/सिकुड़ना): Means to enter into a formal agreement, or to become smaller; it does not collocate with "ticket" in this context.

• Option 3: conform (अनुरूप होना): Means to comply with rules, standards, or expectations; it does not fit the context of a ticket.

• Option 4: convention (परंपरा/सम्मेलन): This is a noun (meaning a custom or a formal assembly), not a verb, so it cannot grammatically fill the blank after "To".

NOTE

• Commonly confused words: confirm (to verify/make certain), conform (to comply with), contract (to agree/shrink), convention (a custom or gathering) — each has a distinct meaning and usage.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
My brother received / his MBA degree into / the university last year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. his MBA degree into.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the preposition "into". The correct preposition to use with the verb "receive" (something) from (a place/source) is "from", not "into".

• Rule — Preposition Usage: we say "receive something FROM somewhere/someone", since "from" indicates the source from which something is obtained.
◦ Correct: My brother received his MBA degree from the university last year.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the university last year" contains no error; it correctly names the source and time.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect since there is indeed a preposition error in the sentence, as explained above.

• Option 4: "My brother received" contains no error; the subject and verb agree correctly.

NOTE

• Commonly confused prepositions in SSC exams: receive/graduate FROM (a place), arrive AT (a small place)/arrive IN (a city or country), depend ON, married TO.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Mobile phones or smartphones are becoming popular all over the world.
B. But at the same time, it also harms us in many ways.
C. It is the most widely used means of communication today.
D. Today, it is very affordable and available to everyone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ACDB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence A is the ideal opener — it introduces the topic in general terms: mobile phones/smartphones becoming popular worldwide.

• Sentence C logically follows A, explaining one reason for this popularity — it is the most widely used means of communication.

• Sentence D follows next, adding a further supporting reason — it is affordable and available to everyone.

• Sentence B is the ideal closer — the word "But" signals a contrast, introducing the paragraph's concluding twist that mobile phones also cause harm, which fits best as a concluding contrasting statement.

• Rule — Paragraph Coherence: the sequence must move from a general introduction to specific supporting points, with the contrasting statement (marked by "But") placed logically at the end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 (ACDB).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ABCD) is incorrect because it places the contrasting sentence B immediately after the opener A, before any positive points about smartphones are established.

• Option 2 (DACB) is incorrect because it begins with a specific supporting detail (D — affordability) before the topic itself (A — popularity) has been introduced.

• Option 3 (CABD) is incorrect because it starts with C, which uses "It", a pronoun that has no antecedent until "mobile phones" is mentioned in A.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, contrast connectors like "But", "However", "Yet" almost always introduce a sentence that comes later in the sequence, never the opening sentence.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given phrase.
Incapable of being defeated
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Invincible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Invincible" means too powerful to be defeated or overcome. (अजेय)
◦ Example: The champion team seemed invincible throughout the tournament.

• This directly matches the given phrase "Incapable of being defeated".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Invisible (अदृश्य): Means unable to be seen; unrelated to the idea of being undefeated.

• Option 2: Unavoidable (अपरिहार्य): Means unable to be avoided or prevented; this refers to inevitability, not to being undefeated.

• Option 4: Ineluctable (अवश्यंभावी): Means unable to be resisted or avoided (used especially for fate); again this refers to inevitability, not to being unbeatable in a contest.

NOTE

• Other similar one-word substitutes: Indomitable (impossible to subdue or defeat, especially of spirit/will), Unconquerable, Impregnable (a fortress/place that cannot be captured by force).

question:
Select the option that correctly expresses the following sentence in passive voice.
Who invited you to this party?
option_1: By whom you are invited to this party?
option_2: By whom are you invited to this party?
option_3: By whom you were invited to this party?
option_4: By whom were you invited to this party?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. By whom were you invited to this party?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Who invited you to this party?" is a Wh-question in the Simple Past Tense, where "who" (the unknown subject) is being asked about.

• Rule — Passive Voice of Wh-questions (Simple Past Tense):
◦ Active: Who + V2 + Object?
◦ Passive: By whom + was/were + Subject + V3? (with subject-auxiliary inversion, as required in questions)

• Applying the rule: the object "you" becomes the subject; since "you" takes "were"; "invited" becomes the past participle "invited" (V3); and "who" becomes "by whom", with the auxiliary "were" inverted before the subject "you" to form a correct question.
◦ Passive: By whom were you invited to this party?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "are" is Present Tense, but the original sentence is in the Simple Past Tense; it also lacks the required subject-auxiliary inversion for a question.

• Option 2 is incorrect because, although it has correct inversion ("are you"), it uses the wrong tense — "are" instead of "were".

• Option 3 is incorrect because it uses the correct tense ("were") but fails to invert the auxiliary and subject ("you were" instead of "were you"), which is required to form a grammatically correct question.

NOTE

• In passive Wh-questions, always check two things together: the correct auxiliary for the tense, and correct subject-auxiliary inversion, since a passive sentence formed from a question must still read as a question.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error in the usage of the interjection.
He replied / in a dry tone, / "Ouch! I will not work / for you anymore."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. "Ouch! I will not work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ouch!" is an interjection used specifically to express sudden physical pain.

• Rule — Interjections: an interjection must match the emotion actually being conveyed by the sentence that follows it. Here, the speaker is expressing defiance/refusal ("I will not work for you anymore"), not physical pain, so "Ouch!" is the wrong interjection for the context — a word like "Never!" or "No!" would have been appropriate instead.

• Additionally, the sentence is spoken "in a dry tone", which further supports that this is a sarcastic/defiant remark, not a cry of pain.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in a dry tone," contains no error; it correctly describes how the sentence was spoken.

• Option 2: "He replied" contains no error; the subject-verb structure is correct.

• Option 3: "for you anymore.\"" contains no error; it correctly completes the quoted sentence with appropriate punctuation.

NOTE

• Common interjections and the emotions they express: Ouch/Ah (pain), Wow/Hurray (joy/excitement), Alas (grief/sorrow), Oh (surprise), Hush (a request for silence), Well (a pause/hesitation).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Gandhi, (1)_________ father of the Indian nation, practiced 'ahimsa' in his personal and political life. He firmly believed that non-violence is not meant merely for monks, saints and priests; it is for commoners too. If violence is the law of the (2)________-beasts, non-violence is the law of the civilised human species. 'The spirit of the brute is inactive and so he knows no law; he knows only physical might. The dignity of man requires obedience to a higher law, to strength of the spirit,' Gandhi said. Ahimsa, to Gandhiji, meant that one should love all; even (3)________ enemies. And the expression of love, ahimsa, should be in such a manner that it impresses itself indelibly upon the so-called enemy, and then the enemy must return that love. It is a practically (4)_________ philosophy. Gandhi was realistic; he believed that non-violence provides the fullest protection to one's self-respect and sense of humour. It won't work in the defence of (5)________ gains and immoral acts. He called his marches off when people indulged in violence during protests for India's freedom. His faith in 'ahimsa' played an influential role in enabling the creation of an independent India in 1947, with minimum bloodshed, breaking the shackles framed by the British.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in the phrase **"Gandhi, (1)___ father of the Indian nation", where "father of the Indian nation"** is a unique title/epithet referring specifically to Gandhi.

• Rule — Definite Article "the": the definite article "the" is used before a noun or title that refers to something/someone unique or specifically identified, such as unique titles, positions, or superlative-type descriptions (e.g., "the Prime Minister", "the Sun", "the father of the nation").

• Since Gandhi is uniquely known as "the father of the Indian nation" (not one among many), the definite article "the" is required.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "an" is incorrect; the indefinite article implies one of several fathers of the nation, which is factually and grammatically wrong for a unique title.

• Option 2: "for" is incorrect; it is a preposition and does not fit grammatically before the noun phrase "father of the Indian nation".

• Option 4: "a" is incorrect for the same reason as "an" — the indefinite article does not suit a unique, singular title.

NOTE

• "The" is used before unique persons/things (the Sun, the Earth), superlatives (the best), and well-known unique titles/epithets (the Father of the Nation, the President).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Gandhi, (1)_________ father of the Indian nation, practiced 'ahimsa' in his personal and political life. He firmly believed that non-violence is not meant merely for monks, saints and priests; it is for commoners too. If violence is the law of the (2)________-beasts, non-violence is the law of the civilised human species. 'The spirit of the brute is inactive and so he knows no law; he knows only physical might. The dignity of man requires obedience to a higher law, to strength of the spirit,' Gandhi said. Ahimsa, to Gandhiji, meant that one should love all; even (3)________ enemies. And the expression of love, ahimsa, should be in such a manner that it impresses itself indelibly upon the so-called enemy, and then the enemy must return that love. It is a practically (4)_________ philosophy. Gandhi was realistic; he believed that non-violence provides the fullest protection to one's self-respect and sense of humour. It won't work in the defence of (5)________ gains and immoral acts. He called his marches off when people indulged in violence during protests for India's freedom. His faith in 'ahimsa' played an influential role in enabling the creation of an independent India in 1947, with minimum bloodshed, breaking the shackles framed by the British.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. forest-living.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"the law of the (2)___-beasts", which is contrasted with "the civilised human species"** later in the same sentence.

• Rule — Compound Adjectives with Present Participles: a noun + present participle (e.g., forest-living) commonly forms a compound adjective describing a habitual state or place of existence, matching the sense of wild animals that live in forests as opposed to civilised humans.

• "Forest-living beasts" correctly and naturally describes wild animals inhabiting forests, fitting the passage's contrast between brute/animal law and civilised human law.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "life" is incorrect; it does not function grammatically as a compound adjective before "beasts" ("life-beasts" is meaningless).

• Option 3: "forest-lived" is incorrect; the past participle form "lived" is not the correct way to form this compound adjective — the present participle "living" is required to express a continuing/habitual state.

• Option 4: "alive" is incorrect; "alive" is a predicative adjective (used after a linking verb, e.g., "the beast is alive") and cannot be used directly before a noun as "alive-beasts".

NOTE

• Other common noun + present-participle compound adjectives: forest-dwelling, sea-faring, law-abiding, English-speaking, record-breaking.

If violence is the law of the (2)________-beasts, non-violence is the law of the civilised human species. 'The spirit of the brute is inactive and so he knows no law; he knows only physical might. And the expression of love, ahimsa, should be in such a manner that it impresses itself indelibly upon the so-called enemy, and then the enemy must return that love. It is a practically (4)_________ philosophy. Gandhi was realistic; he believed that non-violence provides the fullest protection to one's self-respect and sense of humour. His faith in 'ahimsa' played an influential role in enabling the creation of an independent India in 1947, with minimum bloodshed, breaking the shackles framed by the British.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. one's.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"one should love all; even (3)___ enemies"**, where a possessive form is required before the noun "enemies".

• Rule — Possessive of the Indefinite Pronoun "One": when the generic/indefinite pronoun "one" is used as the subject earlier in a sentence, the correct possessive adjective to refer back to it is "one's" (not "his", "her", or "its"), to maintain gender-neutral and grammatical agreement.

• Applying the rule: "one should love all; even one's enemies" correctly agrees with the earlier subject "one".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "her" is incorrect because it wrongly assigns a specific feminine gender to the generic, gender-neutral pronoun "one".

• Option 2: "its" is incorrect because "its" is used for non-human/inanimate antecedents, not for the personal indefinite pronoun "one".

• Option 4: "one" is incorrect because it is the subject/generic form, not the possessive form required before the noun "enemies".

NOTE

• The pronoun "one" takes "one's" as its possessive form and "oneself" as its reflexive form, e.g., "One should always do one's duty and take care of oneself."

And the expression of love, ahimsa, should be in such a manner that it impresses itself indelibly upon the so-called enemy, and then the enemy must return that love. His faith in 'ahimsa' played an influential role in enabling the creation of an independent India in 1947, with minimum bloodshed, breaking the shackles framed by the British.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. proven.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"It is a practically (4)___ philosophy"**, where an adjective is required to describe the noun "philosophy", following the determiner "a" and the adverb "practically".

• Rule — Adjectival Use of Past Participles: "proven" functions as an adjective (meaning demonstrated to be true, effective, or reliable through practice/experience), and adjectives formed this way are placed directly before the noun they qualify (a proven method, a proven fact, a proven philosophy).

• The passage explains that ahimsa has been shown, in practice, to work — hence "a practically proven philosophy".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "prove" is incorrect; this is the base verb form and cannot function as an adjective before a noun.

• Option 2: "approved" is incorrect; it means officially sanctioned or authorised, which is not the intended meaning here (the passage is about the philosophy being demonstrated to work, not officially approved by an authority).

• Option 4: "proving" is incorrect; the present participle would suggest an ongoing, incomplete process ("in the process of proving"), whereas the context requires an already-established, settled quality.

NOTE

• Distinguish "proven" (used as an adjective before a noun, e.g., a proven fact) from "proved" (used as the past participle in verb phrases, e.g., "has proved"); both are acceptable past participles of "prove", but "proven" is preferred adjectivally.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"It won't work in the defence of (5)___ gains and immoral acts"**, where the missing word must describe "gains" in a way that parallels "immoral acts".

• "Ill-gotten" means acquired by dishonest, unfair, or illegal means, and "ill-gotten gains" is a well-established fixed collocation in English.

• This fits perfectly, as the sentence pairs it with "immoral acts" — both describe wrongdoing that non-violence (ahimsa) will not defend or protect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "relevant" is incorrect; it means pertinent or applicable, which does not fit the sense of wrongfully acquired gains.

• Option 3: "ill-will" is incorrect; "ill-will" is a noun meaning hostility or malice, and it does not grammatically or logically combine with "gains" ("ill-will gains" is meaningless).

• Option 4: "moral" is incorrect; it is the opposite of the intended meaning — the sentence is about non-violence refusing to defend wrongful gains, not moral ones.

NOTE

• "Ill-gotten gains" is a common fixed expression referring to money or benefits obtained through dishonest or illegal means. Other similar "ill-" compounds tested in SSC exams: ill-fated, ill-tempered, ill-mannered, ill-equipped.
